accuracy.reason: Primary sources support routing, health sampling/fail-open, state isolation, drain deadlines and atomic retry limits. Diagrams show reverse-proxy return and no migration of in-flight work.

evidence.quote: Health-based routing reduces exposure to failure; it cannot guarantee every request succeeds.

mechanisms.reason: Cards identify routing units and actors, eligibility changes, independent process memory, connection-aware drain and shared transactional deduplication; learner traces all failure cases.

evidence.quote: In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none.

coherence.reason: Request path precedes routing unit, policy and readiness; session ownership precedes drain and retry failure; final capacity view connects the entire serving path.

evidence.quote: Choose the routing unit and required HTTP visibility before choosing a balancing policy.

decisions.reason: Conditional algorithms expose imperfect workload signals; affinity/shared-state costs, spare capacity and reachable alternate entry path prevent redundancy being mistaken for availability. Card 1 also gives a no-balancer case.

evidence.quote: Redundant components alone do not guarantee an available service.

clarity.reason: L4/L7, TLS termination, readiness, affinity, in-flight work, deduplication and headroom are explained at use; short examples expose unequal cost and unknown write outcome.

evidence.quote: a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.

outcomes.reason: C1-C4: learner traces both directions through proxy, chooses readable HTTP L7 with TLS termination, contrasts reused L4 connection and identifies when one server suffices; cards 1-2 teach all.

C1-C4: learner explains all three policy signals and limits, uses capacity/workload-conditioned choices, rejects API scaling as database relief, and requires reachable alternate entry plus surviving headroom; cards 3,8 support the reasoning.

C1-C4: learner distinguishes process answer from useful database-dependent readiness, explains intervals/coverage and post-check failure, limits removal to later selections, and rejects in-flight rescue; card 4 includes all-unhealthy exception.
C1-C3: learner identifies inaccessible/lost A-only cart, affinity benefit with skew and no replication, and shared-storage access with dependency/coordination cost; card 5 supports all.

C1-C3: learner orders cutoff, bounded completion and termination, warns deadline interruption, and handles reused connections versus accepted L7 requests; card 6 and its diagram explicitly reject automatic work transfer.

C1-C4: learner preserves timeout uncertainty, stable shared durable key/result, atomic unique record plus effect, explains new-key/local-memory failure and bounded delayed retry load; card 7 directly teaches each requirement.

sourceChecks.claim: Live AWS ELB overview confirms distribution and redundant backend serving; reverse-proxy request/response diagram is explicitly scoped, avoiding a claim about all balancer architectures.

Live Azure load-balancing overview confirms L7 HTTP paths/TLS offload versus L4 transport. AWS NLB introduction confirms a TCP connection stays on one target; backend encryption is separately configured.
Live nginx HTTP balancing documents turns, fewest active connections and weights; weighting is a traffic share, not live work measurement or performance guarantee.
Live AWS target health docs confirm interval/threshold sampling and all-unhealthy fail-open; removal cannot rescue already-running application work.
Live ASP.NET web-farm docs explain state sharing and cross-node failures; affinity routes but does not replicate A memory. Shared storage has its own access/availability cost.

Live AWS target-group attributes confirm stopping new requests, bounded deregistration delay and possible errors on premature termination. Combined with NLB connection pinning, connection-aware drain warning is sound.
Live AWS idempotent APIs supports stable client ID, durable recognition and atomic token/mutations; Google SRE retry budgets corroborate overload limits.

Live Google SRE handling-overload explains shared resource limits, shedding and retry amplification. AWS redundant serving requires a reachable entry; capacity and failover are requirements, not guarantees.
